lesson.title: Roots Are Powers Too: Differentiating Fractional Exponents
lesson.summary: The power rule formula extends to fractional exponents such as one half or one third, letting you differentiate square roots, cube roots, and similar expressions using the same n x to the n minus 1 pattern.
lesson.body:
Square roots and cube roots might not look like powers of x at first glance, but they are: the square root of x is x^(1/2), and the cube root of x is x^(1/3), using fractional exponents. Since the power rule formula, the derivative of x^n is n x^(n-1), has already been confirmed for positive whole number exponents and for negative whole number exponents, it is natural to ask whether the same formula continues to work when n is a fraction. It does, and this chapter proves the case n = 1/2 directly from the limit definition.

Let f(x) = the square root of x, written as x^(1/2), defined for x greater than or equal to 0. Apply the limit definition: the difference quotient is [square root of (x+h) minus square root of x] / h. This expression cannot be simplified by ordinary algebra the way polynomial or reciprocal expressions can, because square roots do not distribute over subtraction. The standard trick is to multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate expression, square root of (x+h) plus square root of x, which does not change the value of the fraction since it is really multiplying by 1. In the numerator, [square root of (x+h) minus square root of x] times [square root of (x+h) plus square root of x] follows the difference of squares pattern, giving (x+h) minus x, which is simply h. So the whole difference quotient becomes h divided by {h times [square root of (x+h) plus square root of x]}. The factor of h cancels top and bottom, leaving 1 divided by [square root of (x+h) plus square root of x].

Now take the limit as h approaches 0. The square root of (x+h) approaches the square root of x, so the denominator approaches square root of x plus square root of x, which is 2 times the square root of x. The limit is therefore 1 / (2 times the square root of x), which can be rewritten as (1/2) times x^(-1/2). This matches the power rule formula n x^(n-1) with n = 1/2 exactly, since (1/2) times x^((1/2)-1) is (1/2) times x^(-1/2).

For a worked numeric example using a different fractional exponent, consider f(x) = x^(1/3), the cube root of x, with derivative f'(x) = (1/3) x^(-2/3) by the same extended power rule. Evaluate this at x = 8. Since the cube root of 8 is 2, x^(1/3) at x = 8 equals 2, and x^(2/3) equals 2 squared, which is 4, so x^(-2/3) equals 1/4. The derivative is therefore (1/3) times (1/4), which is 1/12. So the tangent line to the cube root curve at x = 8 has slope 1/12, a small positive number reflecting how slowly the cube root function grows for larger x.

With positive whole number exponents, negative whole number exponents, and now fractional exponents all confirmed, the power rule formula n x^(n-1) applies uniformly across every rational exponent you are likely to encounter, always keeping in mind the domain restrictions each specific exponent requires, such as x greater than 0 for exponents like x^(-1/2) where a square root appears in the denominator.
